title: Human Life after Contact with Extraterrestrial Intelligence – An overview of some results from an international survey of public perceptions
byline: Michael Bohlander, Andreas Anton and John Elliott - 17 November 2026 Health and social policy
excerpt: Michael Bohlander, Andreas Anton and John Elliott present findings from an international survey of around 6,500 people on how humanity would respond to contact with extraterrestrial intelligence. Most respondents would be more excited than worried, but a minority would be willing to trade away some human rights in exchange for alien technology.
content:
Michael Bohlander, Andreas Anton and John Elliott present findings from an international survey of around 6,500 people on how humanity would respond to contact with extraterrestrial intelligence. Most respondents would be more excited than worried, but a minority would be willing to trade away some human rights in exchange for alien technology.

In mid- to late 2024, we carried out a survey to canvass global views about what the future for humans would look like once contact with extraterrestrial intelligence (ETI) had been made. This blogpost presents an overview of some of the findings. The full results are available online in an open access pre-print format. The multilingual survey (English, French, German, and Spanish) was not only covering questions such as whether people believe in the existence of aliens etc., but chiefly addressed their expectations of how diverse kinds of contact would affect them personally, and how they thought the human relationship with an alien species could develop. 

Regrettably, the aim of the survey of finding voices from outside the euro-centrically influenced hemisphere, could not be achieved: Of the roughly 6,500 valid responses, Germany, France, the USA and the UK alone delivered 81.6% of all responses. Another 9.6% went to the remaining six of the top ten countries by response-rate, which takes the cumulative value of all top ten countries to 91.2%. The remaining 78 countries from which responses were received were left with 8.8%, i.e. around 0.1% each on average. The survey results are thus culturally skewed. There was an equally drastic imbalance as far as the gender representation was concerned, with males at 75.2%, females at 22.1% and diverse respondents at a mere 1.1% of the total sample. Education levels ranged in the double figures from secondary school leavers to academic degrees, including PhD level, with all other levels at lower single figures. As far as spirituality was concerned, the majority (52.2%) did not identify as spiritual, as opposed to 35.7% who did. Gender, education and spirituality had a discernible impact in some questions.

77.6% of the entire sample agreed or strongly agreed that contact with ETI will be made, and a total of 59.5% were of the view that ETI had already visited Earth. The willingness to accept either scenario declined in direct proportion to the increase in educational level; the scenario of past visits by ETI achieved an overall lower rating. The average for the first question across all levels of spirituality was 48.9%, for the second question 38.3%. 

The question about reacting to a signal from space produced the somewhat unexpected finding, that roughly a cumulative three quarters of respondents would be excited in the first place, whereas only 23.9% would be worried, with overlaps possible due to the multiple answer option. The proportion of those who would be excited rose to over 78% in the scenario about an artefact on the moon, with a roughly equal drop in those concerned – despite the logical consequence that ETI were once close to the Earth and thus there was a more imminent chance of possible direct contact. An equally “relaxed” attitude could be seen regarding an alien spacecraft in Earth’s orbit, when over 63% would just keep watching the news and otherwise continue as usual, with about 45% at least taking the precaution of getting a stockpile of food.

There was a surprising result that quite a high number believed that humans had been contacted, abducted or experimented upon by ETI, with 52.9% of the total respondents believing that humans had been contacted, 37.3% that humans had been abducted and still 34.5% that humans had been experimented upon. Female respondents had the highest values in all three scenarios. The data showed a trend that the higher the level of education, the lower the affirmative answer rate was to all three alternatives. There was also a decline in numbers in proportionality to the degree of spirituality. The numbers were particularly high for respondents who agreed or strongly agreed to being spiritual persons. Over twice as many respondents who tended to consider themselves spiritual agreed to the allegation of experiments having occurred, as opposed to those who did not.

Addressing the origin of UFOs, the extraterrestrial hypothesis was favoured by a clear majority, followed by secret human technology and the interdimensional hypothesis at almost equal levels. Natural phenomena and time travel were also fairly equal, with the idea that UFOs come from unknown regions of the Earth at a distant fifth. Regarding education, support for the extraterrestrial hypothesis lay above70% until the level of university postgraduate degrees, when the numbers dropped into the high 60s, with the post-doctoral level as an outlier at 58.3%. 

Regarding the reaction humanity should choose once an alien craft has landed on Earth, roughly equal at about 81 – 82% were the alternatives to wait and observe, and to send a message of welcome while attempting to communicate. At a clear joint second place over 21% down from the first two were the options of either sending a probe or a team of humans to investigate the spacecraft. Only 13.4% approved of the option of trying to destroy the craft outright. When asked how they would characterise the impact severity of different contact scenarios, from the discovery of microbial life on another planet to an alien spacecraft crewed by biological entities arriving on Earth, within the most serious categories “severe” and “existential”, the responses showed that while the answers involving the clear presence of an intelligent civilisation moved overall rather predictably from a signal from outer space (49.1%) to the spacecraft crewed by biological entities arriving on Earth (89.3%), there was a reversal in the two scenarios of finding a derelict artefact on Earth (63.0%) and of observing an active alien craft within the solar system (73.5%). 

Approval for increasing military space defence capacity to prepare for hostile contact was low. 54.2% in total disagreed or strongly disagreed. Only 28.8% agreed or strongly agreed that humanity should prepare. Asked whether we should disregard the rules of humanitarian law when engaged in hostilities with ETI, especially if the ETI were technologically superior, 66.4% of all respondents agreed or strongly agreed, with only 16% disagreeing.

Regarding a peaceful contact scenario in which the ETI attach a set of conditions to handing over advanced and planet-saving technology to humanity which would entail a violation of human rights, most responses in favour or strongly in favour remained in the single digits. However, freedom of religion and the ban on the use of intrusive methods of criminal investigation were seen as expendable by about roughly a quarter of respondents. The use of birth control measures on humans by ETI quite concerningly still found almost 11% in favour of the abdication of the human species’ self-governance of its own procreation. The question on delivering humans for experiments against their will had 6.2% overall in favour, i.e., a violation of the law against degrading treatment as regulated, for example, in Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which is absolute, with no exceptions even in times of war or national emergency. This value should have been zero across the board, at the very least in Europe. 

The survey, despite its limitations, has hopefully provided some arguments for the future debate about how humanity would react to contact with an extraterrestrial intelligence or civilisation. Although it was designed to deal primarily with the SETI version of contact, we hope that it will also be of use in the discussion about the currently hotly contested problem of UAP disclosure and the risk of so-called “ontological shock” when humans find out that they are not alone in the universe, or indeed on Earth. If the survey findings show anything, it is that humanity will be more adaptable in the case of non-hostile contact than is commonly feared. 

Professor Michael Bohlander holds the Chair in Global Law and SETI Policy at Durham Law School, UK.

Dr. Andreas Anton is a sociologist and research fellow at the Institute for Frontier Areas of Psychology and Mental Health (IGPP) in Freiburg, Germany.

Dr John Elliott is the Coordinator of the SETI Post Detection Hub and a research fellow at the School of Computer Science, University of St Andrews, UK.

The survey is part of the book “Human Life after Contact with Extraterrestrial Civilisations - Interdisciplinary perspectives on the consequences of first contact", co-edited by the authors and Ms Amber Dagnall LLB LLM, PhD candidate at Durham Law School, and forthcoming with Routledge Publishers.
